Still to do

Using the tracer

What this is. A published plate sits underneath. Everything the atlas knows about the geography sits on top of it as points you can drag. Fix what is wrong, press Save, and send me the file.

The backdrop

Plate shows the published sheets — what you are tracing from. Atlas shows the finished map as the phone will draw it, from the geography as it stands this second — what you are tracing towards. The slider fades whichever you have chosen, so you can bring your points forward or push them back. Switching to Atlas is the quickest way to see whether an edit actually improved anything.

The Atlas backdrop redraws as you work, but not while you are mid-drag — it holds the last picture until you let go, so dragging stays smooth.

It is the atlas's own engine, not a copy of it. The palette, the drawing and the label placement are held here word for word as the phone holds them, and a check refuses to build if the two ever differ. The status line names the engine — engine 2026-08-30a — so the sheet in front of you says which one drew it. This matters because the copy in here was once two rounds behind: it had no wave marks, no ground, no canopy, its shore hatching ran inland and its seats were lettered in realm ink. An edit judged against that backdrop was being judged against the faults.

The plates

The top row picks which published sheet you are working against. The Six Duchies plate defines the world; the others are laid over it. Place mode moves the chosen plate — drag to shift it, scroll to scale it about the pointer, [ and ] to turn it half a degree at a time. Nothing else on the sheet moves while you do. The plate you are on is outlined and drawn at full strength; the rest sit back. Where a plate's placement is a guess it says so when you pick it.

Layers, and the “Other layers” button

The atlas keeps its geography in eight separate layers — coast, rivers, ice, relief, woods, places, names, lakes. You edit exactly one at a time: the one lit up. Every tool, every click and every keystroke applies only to that layer.

Other layers is only about what you can see. Switched on, the seven layers you are not editing are drawn faintly behind, so you can line a river up against the coast it runs to. Switched off, they vanish and you see nothing but the layer you are working on, which is the better way to work when the sheet is crowded. It never changes the data, and it never changes what you can click — you can only ever pick points on the layer you are editing, lit or not.

Getting about

Two fingers on the trackpad scroll the sheet; pinch, or hold ⌘ and scroll, to zoom. Space and drag pans from anywhere. Whole sheet frames the entire geography — which is now a good deal more than the first plate, so it no longer opens on a corner of its own map — and Fit plate frames whichever published sheet you are working against. Point handles appear past about 1.6×.

Drawing

Draw traces with the mouse. The stroke is resampled to an even spacing and every point pulled onto the nearest dark ink, so a rough hand still lands on the engraved line. If the stroke begins and ends on a line that is already there, it replaces that stretch instead of starting a new one — which is how a bad piece of coast gets mended. Start or end away from any line and you get a new one.

On the Woods layer, Draw is a brush. Drag over an area and it scatters trees through it, the way a forest actually sits, rather than laying them in a line. Two sliders set it. Brush is how wide the stroke is, shown by the ring under the pointer. Density is how close together the trees sit — the number beside it is the spacing they come out at, in world units.

9 – 12 ua thin scatter; open country with a few trees on it
6.3 uabout what the plate's own engraver drew — the 517 trees read off the sheet sit a median of 6.3 apart
4 – 5 ucloser than the plate; solid woodland
2.5 – 3.5 ua thicket

It is a spacing, not a rule. A wood that keeps one exact distance everywhere reads as a lattice, not a wood. The plate's own trees have a spacing whose spread is about two thirds of its mean — thickets in some places, glades in others, and pairs standing almost touching. The brush does the same: the density rises and falls over the ground on a field about thirty units across, some patches are left as clearings, and about a quarter of the trees get a companion set close beside them. The number you set is what the spacing averages out at.

The brush plants nothing in the sea: the part of a stroke that crosses water is left alone, and it says so. And a thin setting brushed over ground that is already dense will lay almost nothing, which is correct rather than broken — rub it out first with ⌥ if you want to start again.

Attach and Detach

Attach takes two points and will always do something with them — there is no longer such a thing as a point it refuses.

two loose endsthe two lines become one
both ends of one lineit closes into a ring
an end, then anywherethe end moves onto that spot; on rivers the meeting is recorded as runs into…
two middlesthe first point moves onto the second, so the lines meet — they stay two lines

Detach is one click, not two. Arm it, click a point, and the line comes apart there: a ring opens into a line, a line becomes two. Any point will do — there is no minimum distance any more. To cut out a stretch rather than make a single cut, select the points and press ⌫.

Naming, and “shown at”

Select any point and the panel at the foot of the sidebar names what it belongs to — a river with its name, its width and the zooms it appears at; a lake; a place with its kind and realm; a label's text.

Shown at is a pair: the widest view a thing appears at, and the closest. The atlas has four scales, and a fifth answer that is not a scale at all:

0 · whole realmthe opening view. Realms, seas, capitals — what a world plate carries and nothing else.
1 · regiona duchy or two on screen. Duchy names, market towns, the great rivers, the larger isles.
2 · closevillages, lesser rivers and lakes, small isles, the watchtowers.
3 · harbourthe scale of a chart of one bay: quays, ledges, bluffs, anything only a harbour plan would draw.
4 · never drawndrawn at no scale. The thing is kept — named, placed, searchable — but the sheet never letters or marks it.

Never drawn is a single answer, so the second box goes away when you choose it. Use it for what belongs in the atlas but not on the map: a place the books name once and never site, a river we know of and cannot place, the second of two names for one thing, anything that would only crowd the sheet. It is still found by searching here, and when the atlas has a gazetteer and a search of its own it will be found there too, and can be shown when it is deliberately asked for. Nothing is lost by choosing it — pick a scale later and it appears.

A name you placed by hand is its own thing with its own setting: hiding a river does not hide a name anchor sitting on it, so set that to never drawn too if you want the whole of it gone.

In this tracer a hidden thing is still drawn, faint and dashed, so you can see what you have put away. One combination is worth avoiding, and Still to do will say so: never drawn and unnamed. Nothing letters it and nothing can search for it, so it is out of reach altogether.

Shown at is the last word. Rivers also carry a rank, worked out from how long they are, which decides the scale a river appears at when you have not said. If you do say, that is what happens — the rank used to override it quietly, so a river you had set to appear at the regional view stayed hidden because of a number nowhere on screen.

Almost everything wants from set to where it should first appear and to left at 3, so that once a thing has arrived it stays. Setting to below 3 makes something vanish again as you close in, which is worth doing only for a name that a better one replaces — the way Six Duchies gives way to Buck and Bearns.

If you are unsure, ask how far out you would need to be before this thing stopped being worth the ink. A duchy seat: about 1. A hamlet: 2. A ledge that uncovers at low water: 3.

Choosing a kind

Every place and every name has a kind, and the kind decides how it is drawn and how early it appears.

On Places:

seatWhere a ruler sits — a duchy's keep or a realm's capital. Drawn with a filled ring, and named from the widest view in. Buckkeep, Jhaampe, Bingtown, Ripplekeep.
townA market town, worth a name once a duchy or two is on screen. Forge, Turlake, Neatbay, Hallerby.
villageA hamlet, a manor or a landing. Named only close in. Withywoods, Old Ferry, Oaksbywater, Ringhill.
towerA watchtower or beacon. Drawn as a small tower rather than a ring, and — unlike everything else — it is drawn whether or not it has a name, because the plate draws it that way too.

The test for seat against town is not size, it is whether anybody rules from there. The test for town against village is whether you would expect it named on a sheet showing a whole duchy.

On Names:

waterAnything wet — seas, bays, coves, channels, shallows. Set italic and letterspaced in water ink.
regionA realm, a duchy, a range, or a tract of country. Small caps, widely tracked, in the realm's ink.
isleAn island, or a group of them under one name. Roman, in the secondary ink.

Choosing a realm

Nothing in this atlas is tinted. No territory is filled in, because filling spills into the sea and muddies the paper. Instead each realm has its own ink, and that ink goes on its settlements' rings and its region names — so the realm you pick is the only thing answering whose is this? It is worth getting right.

sixDuchiesindigo — Buck, Bearns, Rippon, Shoaks, Farrow and Tilth, and the isles off them
mountainpine — Jhaampe and the Mountain Kingdom, beyond the range
outIslandsslate violet — the islands across the northern sea: Zylig, Mayle, Skyrene, Aslevjal
chalcedoxblood — the Chalced States, down the coast south of the Six Duchies
bingtownochre — Bingtown, Trader Bay and the Traders' own coast
rainWildsgreen — the acid river and the cities on it: Trehaug, Cassarick, Kelsingra
pirateIslesplum — the scattered isles: Divvytown, Others' Island, Key Island
jamailliagold — Jamaillia City, Candletown, and the Satrapy's coast
clerresgrey — Clerres and its school, in the far south
noneplain ink — nobody holds it: open sea, and ground no realm claims

If in doubt: whose soldiers would turn up? A bay between two realms takes none, because water is not held. An island belongs to whoever the books say holds it, not to whoever is nearest.

The tools

Move Vdrags a point. On Places and Names a click opens the name.
Select Sdrags a box round as many points as you like. Then drag any one to move the whole set, or ⌫ to remove them. ⇧ adds to a selection; the arrow keys nudge it.
Draw Ttraces a line freehand — or brushes trees, on Woods.
Add Aputs one point down. Click on a line and it goes in between the two nearest points; click off it and it extends whichever line you are working on, from whichever end is nearer. If there is nothing to add to it says so rather than guessing.
Delete Dremoves the point you click.
Place Pmoves the plate underneath, not the geography.
Attach Jsee above.
Detach Xone click, cuts there.
Smooth Mtakes the tremor out of a selected run.
Delete featureremoves the whole thing the selected point belongs to, not just the point.
Newstarts a fresh river, ice shelf, relief patch, lake or place.

1–8 pick a layer, ⌘Z undoes, ⌘A selects everything on the layer, Esc deselects and cancels whatever is armed.

Still to do

Still to do walks the whole geography and lists everything that wants a hand — a river with no name, a lake too small to draw, a place standing in open water, two rivers carrying the same name, an outline whose shoreline flags have come adrift. Each row says roughly where it is, and clicking it takes you straight there: it switches to the right layer, frames the thing, and selects it, so you can name it or mend it on the spot.

The same panel finds things. Type a name into the box and it lists every river, lake, place and label that matches, and clicking one flies you to it.

An empty list means every river, lake, place and name is named, every outline is big enough to draw, and nothing is standing in the sea. That is what finished looks like.

Getting rid of things

Remove takes out the points you have selected, and stops at two, because a line of one point is not a line. Delete feature takes out the whole thing the selected point belongs to — the river, the outline, the lake — which is the only way to be rid of a stray trace. It asks first, names what it is about to delete, and keeps a copy so undo brings it back.

Undo goes back eighty steps and Redo (⇧⌘Z) comes forward again. A fresh edit forks the history, as it should.

Saving, importing, and not losing work

Save writes atlas-geo.json to your downloads. Send it to me and I rebuild the atlas from it.

Import reads one back in — your own save from another day, or one I have sent you. It replaces everything: the geography, and the placement of the plates with it, since where each plate sits is part of the file.

Your work is kept as you go, in the browser's own store, so closing the tab or reloading no longer costs you anything. On opening, the tracer picks up where you left off and says when that was. Revert throws all of it away and goes back to the geography this tracer was built with — it asks first.

If you open a newer tracer with older work still in the store, it will not quietly revive it: it says so and offers it, because silently reviving a stale sheet over a newer one is the one way this could do real damage.

Plate placement is saved too. Where you drag and scale each plate in Place mode is part of the geography file, so it survives a save, an import, and a reload. You should never have to line a plate up twice.

Snap

Snap nudges a point you drop onto dark ink within about five pixels. It is a nudge, not a magnet: on these plates the coastline, its shore hatching, the tree stamps and the lettering are all the same weight of black, so near a word like Seal Bay snapping will happily walk your line into the type. Turn it off when you are working near lettering. It is always off for Names, which belong in open ground.

Smooth is the better tool for a hand-drawn line, because it does not care what the ink looks like. Select a run of points and press it, or just trace — every stroke is smoothed as it is laid down.

The two kinds of coast

Coast comes in two kinds, and you can now change a run from one to the other.

solidShoreline. The plate draws a shore here, so the atlas draws one — an inked coast with its shore hatching offset outside it.
dottedOff the sheet. Land runs on past everything anyone has charted. The atlas fills it as land but strokes no shore and lays no hatching, and feathers it out into the sea instead.

Select a run of coast points and the panel offers Shoreline and Off the sheet. It also tells you how many of the selected points are currently each. The distinction matters: a line drawn along unwalked country would claim a coast nobody has seen, and would make the continent read as an island. The whole western margin below the Rain Wilds is dotted for exactly that reason.

Use it when you extend a coast out past the edge of a plate, or when you mend a stretch that was wrongly marked. If you trace a new line, all of it starts as shoreline; mark the ends off the sheet if that is what they are.

Worth knowing

Rivers, ice and the name anchors are still mine rather than the plates'. The coast, the trees, the relief and the settlement dots were read off the engravings by machine and line up. Those first three are the ones worth your time.
